items.lead: The angle of repose depends on the method.
items.text: Measured as the cone of the same height and volume, the fast cone has 43.5° at 0.25 m (30.5° with 2 m particles) and the detailed cone about 44° at 1 m. The HCP lattice natively builds hexagonal pyramids (faces 62.1°, edges 58.5°, the volume of a 60.9° cone); compressed to 45° its cones reach 44.3° to 45.0° from 1 m to 0.25 m (36.5° with 2 m).

items.lead: Stops at every turning point keep the ridge level.
items.text: With the derived stops the ridge varies by only 0.03 to 0.07 m along the core at 0.25 m and F2 is 3.0 to 5.2 m³ for 5 to 500 layers, as low as for one layer with its start cone. Play the stacking and watch the long section stay flat after every layer.

With turning points that move inwards as the pile grows, F1 is 0.030 to 0.045 instead of 0.066 to 0.074 with fixed ones, because the end cones are built while travelling over the longer early cores instead of while standing.

Between x = 15 m and 45 m the reclaimed quality varies by only 0.003 to 0.007, and beyond 25 layers nothing changes. The linear quality trend of this input is easy to blend; more layers would mainly pay off for fluctuating inputs.

items.lead: The closed form models miss the geometry.
items.text: Mathematical and Smooth have no stockpile geometry: their F1 is off by a factor of 2 to 3 in both directions, every stop lands in a single slice of the mathematical model (F2 around 98 m³), and a cone ends up in one slice.

At 0.25 m Fast and HCP agree on F1 within 0.007 for every pattern, while F2 of the lattice is lower (3.0 to 4.0 m³ against 3.6 to 5.2 m³). Both are C++ and stack and reclaim 323,000 particles in about 0.2 s; with the snapshots for the time slider a run takes 0.6 to 5 s. The Python port of the lattice needed 56 s.

shows the stockpile at any moment of the stacking, with the stacker as a marker. Fast and HCP show exactly the particles stacked so far, Detailed the latest of 32 evenly spaced snapshots plus up to 32 at layer ends. The cross and long sections follow the slider; the output curves always show the finished pile.

chevrons follow the stacking schedule derived in the Entropy note Chevron Stacking Schedule, with stops at every turning point. Fixed turning points stay at the ends of the core, shrinking ones move inwards as the pile grows so that its toe stays in place. For one layer both reduce to the start cone.
the slider removes everything a 45° reclaimer has taken up to that position, so the face shows the layer structure the reclaimer cuts through. The z cut removes the near side of the pile.

Fast and HCP export every particle through the Python library. Detailed shows its height map, the height of the frozen particle centers. Mathematical and Smooth have no geometry: each reclaim slice is drawn as a 45° ridge holding its volume.
standard deviation of the pile height along the core center line at the end of every layer, averaged over the layers.

only the cone and the 1 layer chevron with 1 m particles, dropped from 16 m. The default drop height of half the bed depth equals the pile height, and the pile then grows towards the side the particles are thrown from.
the fast simulator rounds a drop position to the nearest cell index but treats cells as starting at that index, which shifts its piles by half a particle in x and z (1 m with 2 m particles).
